name: Pulse (nightclub)
label: Pulse memorial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pulse Interim Memorial' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of South Orange Avenue and West Esther Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/424550378: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pulse Nightclub' (38 m across).

text.description:
Pulse was a nightclub at 1912 South Orange Avenue, opened on 2 July 2004 by Barbara Poma and Ron Legler. Poma named it in memory of her brother John, who died from AIDS in 1991. On 12 June 2016 the club was the scene of a mass shooting in which 49 people were killed and 58 injured. It remains the deadliest incident of violence against LGBTQ people in US history. The site is now a place of remembrance, and visitors come to pay their respects as much as to take photographs.

The best-known frame has been the building wrapped in a wall of photographs, with the illuminated Pulse road sign close by. A quieter frame shows the names wall and the club's original exterior walls. The side-street corner described below gives a more open view than the Orange Avenue frontage, which helps on a phone, where you can't step back far.

Please note that the City of Orlando bought the property in October 2023 and plans a permanent memorial. Demolition of the building began on 18 March 2026. What you can see, and which parts of the site are open, may therefore differ from this description. Check the official site before you go. Keep your photography simple and respectful, and leave other visitors out of your frame where you can.
text.geographic_location: Pulse stands at 1912 South Orange Avenue in Orlando, at the corner with Esther Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed nearby, so head for 1912 South Orange Avenue by taxi or hired scooter from central Orlando. Ask to be dropped at the Esther Street side of the site. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and wall of photographs. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need to fit in more of the frontage, and keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where lines can bend. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for a close, quiet frame of the names wall without walking up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of South Orange Avenue and West Esther Street (Southwest corner of the site, at the Esther Street entrance). The building and wall of photographs seen from the side street, with a more open angle than the Orange Avenue frontage. From here the building and its wall of photographs are seen from the side street, with a more open angle than the Orange Avenue frontage. The old building lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the building on one of the lines so the wall of photographs leads the eye along the frame. For an alternative, go to the Orange Avenue side to take in the building wrapped by the photo ribbon wall with the illuminated Pulse sign nearby. For a close frame, use the names wall and the original exterior walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the lit sign don't wash out. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail. Skip portrait mode and Live Photos here; a plain, still photograph suits the place better.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight gives the clearest view of the wall of photographs and the names. Late evening suits the illuminated Pulse sign. Whenever you go, check the official site first, because the site is changing.

text.access_note: This is a memorial site that is being redeveloped, so check the official site before you go to confirm what is open and when.

name: Camping World Stadium
label: Camping World Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lake Lorna Doone Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lake Lorna Doone Park' (relation/19098761): edge nearest the subject (660 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/400475584: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Camping World Stadium' (327 m across).

text.description: Camping World Stadium is Orlando's big bowl-shaped football ground, in the West Lakes part of Downtown Orlando. It began life in 1936 as Orlando Stadium, built as a Depression-era public works project, and went on to be known as the Tangerine Bowl and the Florida Citrus Bowl. It has since grown a long way beyond its first 8,900 seats, and by 1989 it could hold 65,438. It still hosts the Citrus Bowl, and it was one of the venues for the 1994 FIFA World Cup. A good place to photograph the stadium from is Lake Lorna Doone Park, just north of it. From the park's lakeside, the stadium rises across the water, with the trail and greenery as foreground. That foreground gives the picture some depth, so it looks like a place rather than just a big wall of seating. If the lake is calm, you may also get some reflection. A second option is Church Street Overlook, which has a lake-level view across Lake Lorna Doone and a citrus-tree design to frame the shot. The stadium is being renovated, with building work focused on the north end until summer 2027, so expect cranes or hoardings in some views. The park's page has also shown a temporary closure notice, so check the park's current status before you set out.
text.geographic_location: In the West Lakes neighbourhood of Downtown Orlando.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so start from Downtown Orlando and head to Lake Lorna Doone Park, just north of the stadium. Once there, the stadium is to the south, across the lake. Check the park's current status and any construction fencing before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole stadium, the lake and the path in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rim of the stadium and the details of the structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lake Lorna Doone Park (north end of the stadium, across the lake). The stadium rising across the lake, with the park's lakeside trail and greenery in the foreground. The nearby Lake Lorna Doone Park and its trail give you the view, with the stadium rising across the water and greenery in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower line so the stadium sits along the upper third. Keep the lakeside trail or some greenery in the bottom corner for depth. If the north-side building work spoils the wide shot, try a tighter 2x-3x frame on the part of the stadium that looks clear. For another angle, try Church Street Overlook, where the overlook's citrus-tree design can frame the stadium.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stadium doesn't wash out. Hold the phone with both hands and keep it level against the gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder, because facing south around midday puts the sun in front of you. On a calm day the lake may give a reflection.

text.access_note: Lake Lorna Doone Park is a city park, but its status can change, so check the City of Orlando's park page before you go. Access around the stadium on event days may differ.

name: Orlando Science Center
label: Orlando Science Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Loch Haven Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Orlando Loch Haven Park' (relation/1213925): edge nearest the subject (851 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/308386066: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Orlando Science Center and Dr Phillips Cinedome' (138 m across).

text.description:
The Orlando Science Center is a hands-on science museum in Loch Haven Park, and its domed, curved front makes a clean, simple photo. The museum began life as the Central Florida Museum, which opened in the park in 1960. The building you see today opened on 1 February 1997 and is about six times larger than the original. Inside are a giant-screen CineDome theatre and an observatory on the sixth floor with Florida's largest public refractor telescope, so the building is bigger than it looks from the lawn.

The best view is from the park lawn opposite the domed front. Large oak trees stand in the foreground, which gives your photo depth and a sense of scale, and the building sits neatly in the middle of the frame. Stand square-on and the symmetry does most of the work for you. If you want a second angle, the curved side of the building catches morning light when seen from the parking area side. The outdoor Finfrock Terrace is said to have views of the downtown skyline behind the building, but it may only be reachable through the museum or at private events, so check access before you go.

Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to line up the dome, and let the oak branches frame the top of the picture.
text.geographic_location: The Orlando Science Center stands in Loch Haven Park in Orlando, Florida. The lawn opposite its domed front is the place to take the photo.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Loch Haven Park in Orlando using your usual local transport. From there the building is straight ahead to the east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the dome and the oak trees both fit naturally. If the building does not fit, step back a few paces before you use the ultra-wide (0.5x), which can stretch the edges. Use 2x if you want a tighter shot of the dome itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Loch Haven Park (lawn across from the domed front facade). The domed facade of the science center framed with large oak trees in the foreground for depth and scale. The building is directly to the east. From here you see the domed facade framed by large oak trees in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the dome and switch on the gridlines so the building sits symmetrically. Let the oak branches fill the top or the sides of the frame to add depth and scale. For a different view, try the curved side of the building from the parking area side, or the skyline from Finfrock Terrace if you can get access.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not turn dark against it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light suits the curved facade when seen from the parking area side. The lawn view is worth trying at any time of day when the building is evenly lit.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is listed as free. Access to Finfrock Terrace and the museum may be restricted, so check the Orlando Science Center website before you go.

name: Lake Eola Park
label: Lake Eola Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lake Eola Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lake Eola Park' (relation/16755658): edge nearest the subject (690 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16755658: large area 'Lake Eola Park' (691 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Downtown lake with the famous fountain and swan boats.

text.description: Lake Eola Park is the public park at the heart of Downtown Orlando, built around a small lake that is really a sinkhole. The photo here is the classic one: the Linton E. Allen Memorial Fountain in the middle of the water, with the downtown towers rising behind it and swan boats often drifting through the frame. The lake is about 23 acres, and a 0.9-mile (1.4 km) path runs all the way round, so you can walk it and try several angles. The fountain dates back to 1912. The current one replaced an earlier version in 1957, was renamed in 1966, and was repaired and rededicated in 2011 after a lightning strike. It changes colour at night like a light show, which makes the park especially good around dusk. From the southeast shore, everything fits in one picture: foreground water, fountain, and skyline. Early in the morning the water can be very still, giving a clean reflection of the towers. Reeds and waterfowl by the edge make a natural foreground. For a closer shot, zoom in on the fountain and photograph it lit up in the evening. Check that the fountain is running before you go.
text.geographic_location: Lake Eola Park is in the South Eola neighbourhood of Downtown Orlando. It is bounded by East Robinson Street, Rosalind Avenue, East Central Boulevard and North Eola Drive.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for the park in Downtown Orlando, which sits right in the middle of the downtown streets. From there the park centre is about 89 m away, roughly a 1-minute walk to the north-west, and the fountain is seen across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the fountain, skyline and water in one frame. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and shoreline. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer behind the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lake Eola Park (southeast shore of the lake). The Linton E. Allen Memorial Fountain sits mid-lake with the downtown skyline rising behind it, framed across the water. From here you look north-west across the water to the Linton E. Allen Memorial Fountain, with the downtown skyline rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, leaving room for the water and reflections. Place the fountain just off-centre and let the towers stand behind it. Catch a swan boat or some reeds at the edge for foreground interest. For a different view, zoom in on the lit fountain for a closer shot, or shoot the reflected high-rises with reeds and waterfowl in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit fountain and the towers do not burn out at dusk. Use night mode once the light fades, and hold your phone against your body or a railing to keep it steady. A Live Photo can capture the movement of the water jets.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise for glassy water and clear reflections, or blue hour for the lit fountain and towers.

text.access_note: Lake Eola Park is a public park and casual phone photos are generally fine, but check the official site before you go, especially for any professional or commercial shoot, which needs a permit.

name: Church Street Station
label: Church Street Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Church Street' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/906950901: the OpenStreetMap point 'Church Street'.

text.description:
Church Street Station is the old Orlando railway depot and the entertainment and dining complex that grew up around it, right in the middle of downtown. The depot dates from 1889, when the South Florida Railroad built it, and it still stands today on the National Register of Historic Places. In 1974 the area began a new life as a nightlife and shopping complex, and it later grew to cover both sides of the tracks. Today it also has a SunRail stop, so the old and the modern sit side by side.

For photos, the stretch along the SunRail tracks, across from Ferg's Depot, is the place to aim for. A plain white wall and a set of stairs make a clean, simple backdrop for portraits and travel snaps, with the station area in the background of the frame. Parking nearby is limited, so it is easiest to arrive without a car if you can. Some of the businesses here may not allow photography inside, so keep to the street and platform-side areas, and ask first if you want to shoot indoors.

If you are still around after dark, the lit streetscape of the complex, with its colourful lights and street life, makes a very different second picture from the same area.
text.geographic_location: Church Street Station is in downtown Orlando, beside the SunRail tracks on Church Street. The old depot and its surrounding buildings form the heart of the complex.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of downtown Orlando and head to Church Street, where the old depot and the SunRail tracks run side by side. By taxi or ride-hail, ask for Church Street Station. The phone icon on the map is right at the spot, so you can walk straight to it once you arrive. Because parking is limited, a drop-off is often easier than driving yourself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural street-level view of the white wall, the stairs and the station area behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole stairway in the frame, or to the 2x telephoto if your phone has one, to pull the station closer for a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Church Street, along the SunRail tracks and across from Ferg's Depot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the white wall level with the vertical lines so the stairs look straight. Place a person on or beside the stairs and leave the station area visible behind them for context. For a second, livelier picture, come back after dark and shoot the lit street with its colourful lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white wall does not turn grey or lose detail. Portrait mode works well for people against the wall. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is simplest for the white wall and stairs, and the evening suits the lit streetscape, using night mode.

text.access_note: This is a street-level area beside the SunRail tracks, but individual businesses may restrict photography and the complex has been redeveloped, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Daylight suits the white wall and stairs because it keeps the white surface evenly lit.
A white wall can look grey or lose detail in bright light unless the exposure is lowered slightly.
Night mode benefits from the phone being held steady.
Arriving without a car or by drop-off is easier because parking is limited.

name: Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts
label: Dr. Phillips Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Seneff Arts Plaza' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sennef Arts Plaza' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts'.

text.description: Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts is Downtown Orlando's main performing arts venue, and its grand opening was on 6 November 2014. It fills two city blocks, so it is a big building to fit into one frame. That is the main thing to plan for when you photograph it. It holds several theatres, including the 2,700-seat Walt Disney Theater. Steinmetz Hall opened in January 2022, and the cabaret-style Judson's Live joined it in January 2024. The open plaza in front gives you room to step back and get the whole facade with the downtown buildings around it. This makes it a good spot for a wide, open-air shot, and also for a group or couple photo with the building behind you. Stand on the plaza and turn towards the building, then choose between a wide view of the whole frontage and a tighter shot of one section. If you are visiting in the evening, the lit sign and glowing facade make a good second set of photos. Keep an eye on people crossing the plaza, as they add scale, but you may need a few tries to get a clear frame. Check what is on before you go, because event days can change how much of the space you can use.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Orlando, on the blocks bordered by Orange Avenue to the west, South Street to the north, Rosalind Avenue to the east and Anderson Street to the south. Magnolia Avenue runs through the middle of the site.
text.directions_text: Head for Downtown Orlando and make your way to the plaza in front of the building. Follow the building's frontage rather than the surrounding streets if you are unsure. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the downtown buildings around it. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural-looking shot of the building with people in front. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lit sign or a detail of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Seneff Arts Plaza. The venue's facade with downtown Orlando around it, framed for a wide, open-air shot of the building. From here you see the venue's facade with downtown Orlando around it, which suits a wide, open-air shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building level so the vertical lines stay straight. Tilt the phone only slightly upwards, as tilting too far makes the building lean. For a group or couple photo, put the people on one third of the frame and leave the building behind them. If you want a different view, the upper level behind the Dr. Phillips sign shows the lit sign and building at night, but it may be limited to ticket holders or event guests.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and any lights do not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone still against your body or a rail. For people in front of the building, portrait mode works best from a short distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good time, as the building's lights start to show against the sky. Earlier in the day is better for a clean, open view of the plaza.

text.access_note: The plaza is described as an open public space used for downtown events, but the upper level and the theatre interiors are on the venue's own grounds, so check the official site before you go.

name: Harry P. Leu Gardens
label: Leu Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rose Garden' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Virginia S Nelson Rose Garden' (way/1381550999): middle (22 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1173248: large area 'Harry P. Leu Gardens' (647 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Botanical gardens with roses, camellias and a historic house.

text.description:
Harry P. Leu Gardens are semi-tropical and tropical gardens in Orlando, covering nearly 50 acres of landscaped grounds and lakes. Trails run beneath 200-year-old oaks and past forests of camellias. Harry and Mary Jane Leu bought the house and 40 acres in 1936, and they brought back exotic plants from their travels, including 240 varieties of camellia. In 1961 they gave the house and gardens to the City of Orlando. The restored Leu House Museum still sits at the heart of the grounds.

For a phone photo, start at the Rose Garden near the main entrance. It is described as one of Florida's largest formal rose gardens, and the neat rows of beds make a natural pattern for a picture. The paths and greenery around the beds act as a frame, so the shot looks composed without much effort. If you have time, the Leu House Museum, seen over the roses, and the shaded Historic Camphor Row are worth a second and third picture. Camphor Row is a walkway under broad camphor canopies, with dappled light on the path.

The roses look best in spring blooms, from late March through May. Outside those months, check what is in bloom before you go, as the oaks, camellias and lakeside views also make good pictures. Take your time, because the best frames here are found by walking slowly and looking back along the paths.
text.geographic_location: The gardens are at 1920 North Forest Avenue, in Orlando, Florida. The Rose Garden is near the main entrance.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stops serve this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or hired scooter from central Orlando. Ask for 1920 North Forest Avenue, the gardens' address. Once through the main entrance, the Rose Garden is close by. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rose beds as you see them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in more rows and the framing foliage. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a single bloom or to compress the rows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rose Garden (near the main entrance). Rows of formal rose beds in bloom, with the gardens' paths and foliage framing the subject. The Rose Garden is reached inside the gardens, near the main entrance. Once you find the beds, stand where you can look across the rows of formal roses, with the garden paths and foliage around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a path along one of the lines so it leads the eye through the beds. Keep a few blooms sharp in the foreground and let the rows fade behind them. If you move on, the Leu House Museum over the roses and Historic Camphor Row with its dappled light make good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap a rose to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich. For close-ups, try portrait mode to soften the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring, from late March through May, when the roses are in bloom.

text.access_note: This is a paid-admission garden, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules, as commercial shoots need prior authorisation and drones may need permits.

name: Orlando Museum of Art
label: Orlando Museum of Art
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/345239051: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Orlando Museum of Art' (143 m across).
notes: Art museum in the Loch Haven Park cultural area.

text.description: The Orlando Museum of Art is a not-for-profit art museum serving Orlando and Central Florida, and its low, spread-out buildings make a calm, uncluttered subject for a phone photo. The museum began in 1924 as the Orlando Art Association, a group of local artists who met informally to show and discuss their work. The current building story started in 1960, when a new home designed by James Gamble Rogers III opened. Later additions came from architects Nils Schweizer and Duane Stark, both students of Frank Lloyd Wright. A renovation finished in 1997 brought the museum to its present size of about 80,000 square feet. On the map the site measures roughly 143 metres across, so there is plenty of building to work with. Inside, the collection includes contemporary art, American art, art of the ancient Americas and African art, though what is on show changes with the exhibitions. For photographs, think of this as an architecture stop. Look for long horizontal lines, the entrance, and any signs or banners that tell people what the building is. Step back so the whole front fits, then move closer for details such as doorways, textures and shadows. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the horizontals look straight. If you want to photograph inside, rules can differ between galleries and exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Orlando, Central Florida. It was called the Loch Haven Art Center from 1960 until 1986.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Orlando and go by taxi or hired scooter to the Orlando Museum of Art. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk. Check the museum's official site for the exact entrance and parking before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the building from a distance, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance, signage or architectural lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The museum is right there, so you are at the centre of the site. Walk a little way back from the building to fit more of it into the frame, and move to the sides for different angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roof and wall edges with the horizontal lines so the building does not look tilted. Include a bit of foreground, such as paving or planting, to give a sense of scale. For a close-up, fill the frame with one doorway or a pattern of light and shadow.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail. If you shoot from a long way back, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and longer shadows that show off the building's shapes. Midday sun can be harsh and flatten the walls.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry to the building is likely to be ticketed and have set hours; check the official site before you go.

name: Orange County Regional History Center
label: History Center
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/47026386: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Orange County Regional History Center' (57 m across).
notes: Historic courthouse building housing a local history museum.

text.description:
The Orange County Regional History Center fills the old Orange County Courthouse in downtown Orlando, a five-storey neoclassical building that was dedicated on 12 October 1927. It was designed by Orlando's first registered architect, Murry S. King, and cost close to a million dollars. King died during construction, so his son James finished the work. The building served as the courthouse for decades, and after a new high-rise courthouse opened in 1995 it was chosen to become a regional history museum, which opened in September 2000. Today it covers local history going back about 2,000 years.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the solid, formal look of an old civic building among newer downtown blocks. Its tall, symmetrical front suits a straight-on shot. Stand back, switch on the gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. If you cannot fit all five floors in at the default lens (1x), try the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level, because it exaggerates any tilt. The telephoto (2x or more) is good for details such as the upper storeys and the stonework. Check the museum's official site before you go if you want to see inside.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of downtown Orlando, inside the historic 1927 Orange County Courthouse building. Heritage Park was later built on the site of the old courthouse annex next to it.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Orlando and ask for the Orange County Regional History Center, which is the old 1927 courthouse. text.description:
Orlando City Hall is the working headquarters of the city government, a nine-floor postmodern building finished in 1992 in downtown Orlando. Its best-known feature is the 120-foot copper dome, and the walls are clad in pale granite-aggregate concrete panels. The architects, Heller Manus, drew on the grand civic buildings of the past, and the dome and the plaza with its steps, palms and flagpoles are why it photographs well. A small piece of film trivia: the previous city hall building was blown up for the opening scene of Lethal Weapon 3 (1992).

The lake and the downtown skyline give you a busier, more interesting background than the building alone. City Hall is about 635 m off to the south-west, so use the park for a wide, scene-setting shot and then walk over to the plaza for the building itself. Keep the dome and the flagpoles in frame, and let the steps and palms lead the eye upwards. Photograph the building from outside, as the inside is generally not open for casual visits.
text.geographic_location: City Hall stands in downtown Orlando at the corner of South Orange Avenue and South Street, within the CNL Center City Commons complex.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot. From the park, City Hall is about 635 m to the south-west. Head for the corner of South Orange Avenue and South Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: At the park, use the default lens (1x) for the lake and skyline, or the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the water and the sky. At City Hall, the ultra-wide (0.5x) fits the plaza, steps and dome together, while the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) picks out the copper dome and the building's detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lake Eola Park (park grounds a short walk east of City Hall; sources do not name a specific spot with a sightline to the building). A nearby setting for a City Hall photo that a guide calls the classic shot in front of the building, with the downtown skyline and lake in the background. A guide calls this the classic setting for a photo in front of City Hall, with the downtown skyline and the lake behind you or your group. For a close shot of City Hall, walk over to its plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines. In the park, put the lake or the skyline on a third and a person or group in the foreground. At the plaza, keep the building's vertical lines straight and include the steps, palms and flagpoles as foreground. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls, and step back so the dome is not cut off at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale walls keep their detail. Use portrait mode for people in the park, and take a few frames in case of passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset at the park, according to several guides that feature it.

text.description: The Mennello Museum of American Art sits in Loch Haven Park beside Lake Formosa, in a former private house that was given to the city of Orlando. That domestic scale is what makes it a pleasant subject for a phone: you are photographing a house-sized building with garden and lake around it, not a large institutional front. The museum opened in 1998 and is owned and run by the city. At its core is a permanent collection of paintings by Earl Cunningham (1893-1977), alongside changing shows of American artists. The grounds also hold a sculpture garden with abstract works by Alice Aycock, which gives you strong shapes and colours to frame against the trees and water. Look for a picture that combines the building, a sculpture and a slice of the lake, so the photo says 'art by the water' at a glance. Walk around the grounds before you settle on a spot, because the sculptures look quite different from each side. Keep people out of the foreground unless they add scale. Photography rules inside the galleries can vary by exhibition, so ask staff or check the official site before you go, and take your main pictures outside, where you have more freedom. Because the phone icon on the map is at the building itself, you can start close and then step back along the grounds to fit more in.

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'East Jefferson Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of North Magnolia Avenue and East Jefferson Street (our map tiles).

text.description:
The Cathedral Church of St. Luke is an Episcopal cathedral in downtown Orlando and the seat of the Diocese of Central Florida. That framing is what makes it a good phone photo: the trees and road give you natural lines and some depth, and the stonework gives you a strong subject.

The story is easy to share with your photo. St. Luke's began as a small faith community in the home of Francis Eppes, who moved to Orlando in 1869, and it was named a cathedral church on 31 March 1902. The present building was designed by the Boston firm Frohman, Robb and Little, who also designed Washington National Cathedral. The cornerstone was laid on 13 April 1925. Money ran short, so a temporary wall stood at the altar end for decades, and the cathedral was only completed in 1986 to 1987. The Florida historical marker for the cathedral stands at this same street corner, so it is worth a quick photo too.

Take one wide shot that includes the street and the trees, then step in for a tighter shot of the façade. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. Wait for a gap in passing traffic or pedestrians if you want a clean view.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in downtown Orlando, on North Magnolia Avenue near its junction with East Jefferson Street.
text.directions_text: From downtown Orlando, head to the corner of North Magnolia Avenue and East Jefferson Street. Walk towards the church along Magnolia Avenue and turn round now and then to check how the trees frame the view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

The church's Gothic Revival front along Magnolia Avenue, with the street and tree canopy leading toward the building. The cathedral is a short walk to the south-west. From here the photo shows the Gothic Revival front along Magnolia Avenue, with the street and tree canopy leading towards the building. It should be the west side of Magnolia Avenue, on the church side when you walk north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame so the tree canopy forms a natural tunnel towards the church. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid leaning walls. Then take a second, tighter shot of the façade, leaving a little sky above the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church on the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case a car or passer-by spoils one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters stonework and avoids harsh midday shadows under the trees. Early in the day the street is likely to be quieter.

text.description:
The Angebilt Building is an 11-storey brick building on North Orange Avenue in downtown Orlando. It was designed by architect Murray S. King and built between 1921 and 1923. It opened on 14 March 1923 as the Angebilt Hotel, with 250 rooms. It later survived hard times, including a fire on the top two floors in 1983, and was converted into offices. Today it has offices upstairs and bars and shops at street level.

A classic view of it is the long, straight view down Orange Avenue. From the Washington Street corner, the brick facade sits at the end of the street, with the downtown scene around it. Orlando Magazine has repeated a 1940s photo from this same corner, so you can echo a historic picture of the building. The straight street also gives you strong lines that lead the eye towards the tower.

Take the first shot at the corner, then walk down for a closer view. A second option is further along North Orange Avenue, where you can capture the building's north-west corner and its full height. Keep the building's vertical lines straight by holding your phone level, and use the gridlines to help. Stay on the pavement and watch for passing traffic while you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: The Angebilt Building is in downtown Orlando, at 37 North Orange Avenue, on the corner of Wall Street. It is one block south of Washington Street.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Orlando and the Washington Street corner on Orange Avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic straight view down the street. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the facade closer without walking into the traffic. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close and want the full height in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of North Orange Avenue and Washington Street (Stand on the Washington Street corner and face south along Orange Avenue). The Angebilt's brick facade at the end of a straight view down Orange Avenue, with the downtown street scene around it. Stand on Orange Avenue at the Washington Street corner and face south along the street. This is the same corner used for a 1940s photo that Orlando Magazine has repeated.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the street's edges so the building sits in the middle of the frame, with the street leading towards it. Hold the phone level to keep the building's vertical edges straight. For a different angle, try a view of the building's north-west corner from further along North Orange Avenue, which shows its full height and street frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't turn into a dark shape. If there are lots of people or cars, take a few shots, or try a Live Photo and pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the street is quiet. Because you are looking south, the street-facing side of the building may be in shade for much of the day, so check the light on the day and try early morning or late afternoon.

text.access_note: The streets around the building are open public space, but the Angebilt is now an office building, so the lobby and interior are not public photo spots; check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

text.description:
The Old Orange County Courthouse is the 1927 courthouse in downtown Orlando. It now houses the Orange County Regional History Center and the Historical Society of Central Florida. It stands near the sites of earlier courthouses: one built in 1892 was demolished in 1957, and a 1960 annex was pulled down in 1998. That layering of old and new is what makes the area interesting to photograph.

It is on the brick walkway and front steps of the newer Orange County Courthouse, a short walk to the north. From there you can take a framed view up the brick path and steps towards the entrance, which suits photos of people walking towards or away from the doors. It is a quieter alternative to a wide front view. You can also photograph the central semicircular entrance with its engraved stone front, and close-ups of the stonework and layered archways.

The 1927 building is a walk to the south. Once you are there, step back across the street if you can, so the whole front fits in the frame. Keep your phone upright for the height of the building and turn it sideways for the full width. Take a few shots at different distances. People walking past give a sense of scale.
text.directions_text: No nearby stations or tram stops are listed for this spot. The old 1927 courthouse lies about 700 m to the south of it. Walk south along the main downtown streets and look for the History Center building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walkway and steps. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the entrance and the 1927 building's front if you are close. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for stonework and archway details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Orange County Courthouse (brick pathway and front steps leading up to the entrance). A framed view up the brick walkway and steps toward the building, useful for shots of people walking toward or away from the entrance. From here you look up the brick path and steps towards the entrance, with the 1927 courthouse lying to the south of you. Stand at the foot of the path so the lines of the bricks lead the eye towards the doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the walkway down the centre or along a third of the frame. Wait for someone to walk along the path and take a few shots as they move. For a different view, photograph the semicircular entrance and engraved stone front with the plaza in the foreground, or move in close on the archways, where the layered openings give depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day, when the light is softer and the stone looks warmer.

text.description:
The Wells'Built Museum is a small African American history museum in the former Wells'Built Hotel, in the middle of Orlando's historic Parramore district. Dr William Monroe Wells, one of the city's first Black doctors, built the hotel in 1921 for African Americans who were barred from Florida's segregated hotels. Performers such as Ella Fitzgerald, Count Basie, Ray Charles and Louis Armstrong stayed here during the segregation era. The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2000, and the museum opened in 2009.

It photographs well because it is a plain, honest street scene with real history behind it: a two-storey brick building with a large glass storefront on West South Street. It is not a grand landmark, so the best pictures show the building in its neighbourhood rather than as a close-up. If you want a straight-on shot of the full brick front, walk along to the entrance and frame it from directly in front.

Photography inside the museum is restricted by exhibit and signage, and flash is discouraged, so ask the staff before you take any pictures indoors. Plan this as a short stop of ten minutes or so outside, and check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of the historic Parramore district of Orlando, at 511 West South Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Parramore district in Orlando and look for West South Street. No rail or tram stops are listed nearby, so check local transport options before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural street-level view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole front in. Use 2x for details such as the glass storefront and the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of West South Street and South Division Avenue (corner with the museum building). The two-story building seen at an angle from the intersection, placing the facade and its corner alongside the street. From here the building appears further down the street to the west. Walk west toward it until you are near the museum's corner, where you can see the two-storey building at an angle, with the front and side alongside the street. The museum entrance lies further along to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and, as you approach, place the building's corner on one of the vertical lines, with the street running off in a diagonal. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For an alternative, walk to the front of the Wells'Built Museum and take the full brick front straight on, with the large glass storefront centred.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brick facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or glass looks washed out. Avoid flash if you go inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the street is lit and the facade is easy to read. Visit on a weekday if you also want to go inside, but check the official site first.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street; the museum inside is a visitor attraction with restricted photography, so check the official site before you go.
